To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spectral excitation of a detector that scattes the beam is given by a sum of terms, two of which are proportional to the flux and contain the information on the signal of interest, while the other two are proportional to the higher powers of the beam flux and contain the noise.

(i) the demodulation of the incident beam is a coherent effect that can be detected by scattering the beam on a detector, and (ii) that the demodulated signal is given by the square of the flux, and that the noise is proportional to the flux.

the spectral excitation rate of a scattering detector is a sum of four distinct terms: The first two (the B terms) contain all the information about the demodulation of the beam, the beat effects and the self-beat; the remaining two (the A terms) contain the information on the inelastic scattering and some coherent corrections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of correlations (and in particular the demodulation of a signal) in a beam by means of a detector that scats the beam.
a theory for the detection of correlations and demodulation in beams of particles by means of a scattering detector.
the demodulation of a beam by a detector that scatterns the beam.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the B terms are the only ones that contain the information on the signal of interest, and that they are the ones that must be extracted from the detector signal.

the theory of the present paper is a natural and simple generalization of the conventional theory of inelastic scattering, in the sense that it contains all the information of the latter as special cases, while adding to it the new effects of the demodulation.

the spectral excitation functions for a scattering detector are determined by the flux, the wavefunction and the stochastic distribution of the beam; they can be written as a sum of two terms, each of which is a function only of these three quantities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the theory is able to explain all the phenomena observed in the scattering of a beam of atoms or molecules, and that it provides a unified description of all these phenomena.
the B terms are a measure of the correlations in a beam and are a natural extension of the conventional scattering cross sections; the A terms are the conventional scattering cross section.
the B terms describe the signal and the A terms the noise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the demodulation of a beam can be detected and analyzed in the presence of noise, and that this can be done by using the spectral excitation of a scattering detector.

a simple and general formula for the demodulation of the incident beam can be given in terms of the incident wave function and the stochastic distribution of the beam, and that the formula is naturally decomposed into a sum of terms that are proportional to the flux and higher powers of the beam flux, with the higher powers containing information on the self-demodulation and Forrester-type beat effects.
the spectral excitation functions of a detector can be decomposed in a very simple and general manner.
